v.why: Raising an already large Adam step size causes divergence and collapsing accuracy, unlike at small or moderate rates.
At tiny learning rates the network is undertrained in 243 epochs, so increasing the rate gives large gains (e.g. +29pp on vehicle).
Deeper ReLU nets are less stable, so a larger step size hurts more (exp 10 vs 9).
Very wide layers amplify effective update magnitude, so raising the learning rate is more damaging (exp 14 vs 13).
Lowering a divergent learning rate recovers training, giving large gains that do not occur at small rates.
Once the L2 penalty is strong, increasing it further causes underfitting and clear accuracy drops, whereas at tiny alpha it is negligible.
Relaxing an overly strong L2 penalty restores model capacity (exp 99, 100), while at small alpha it has no effect.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and stabilize training at high learning rates (exp 23, 26).
Adding layers at high learning rates triggers instability and collapse (exp 59, 62).
Widening the net at high learning rates worsens instability (exp 44, 50), while at moderate rates width changes are near-neutral.

raw:
These hypotheses come from patterns in the 100 single-seed experiments and from known MLP and Adam training behavior.

- **Learning rate is the main driver.** Raising the learning rate when it is already high caused large accuracy losses, up to −77 pp on segment. Deep or wide networks made this worse: compare experiments 10 vs 9 and 14 vs 13. Raising it from the lowest values helped, by up to +29 pp.
- **Larger batches help at high learning rates.** Increasing batch size helped when the learning rate was high (experiments 23 and 26) and hurt when it was very low (experiments 21 and 24).
- **Strong L2 penalty only hurts.** At alpha of 0.0167 or above, raising alpha hurt clearly on all three datasets, and lowering it from 1 helped.
- **Adding capacity is risky at high learning rates.** More depth or width there led to large losses (experiments 44, 50, 59 and 62).
